title: The More I Prepare to Talk About AI, the Less I Talk About AI
author: Jen Shew
source: Leadership at the Edge of Change (jenshew.substack.com), September 2, 2026
summary: Preparing a Board of Trustees workshop on AI for a Christian college abroad, Jen Shew finds herself abandoning technology talk for a much older question: what is education for, and what kind of person is it trying to form? She argues AI sharpens rather than distracts from this question because higher education has long used student-produced artifacts, papers, sermon outlines, presentations, as evidence that learning happened, and now that AI can generate many of those artifacts convincingly, institutions must confront whether the product was ever really the point or merely a proxy for the wisdom, judgment, and character the assignment was supposed to cultivate. Shew is explicit that she resists exporting her own institution's (Lipscomb's) playbook onto a context with a different mission, student community, and economic reality, illustrated by the host college's president recalling how his school once had to deliberately teach computer skills before they were locally available, a role reversed now that AI already sits in every student's pocket and the real task is teaching wise use rather than access. Her conclusion reframes AI strategy as a downstream consequence of institutional identity rather than a technology decision: colleges best prepared for AI will not be the fastest adopters but the ones who know precisely what human formation they refuse to outsource to a tool.
points: Shew's central reframe treats AI not as a distraction from education's deeper questions but as a forcing function for them: because AI can now generate the products (papers, sermon outlines) long used as proxy evidence of learning, institutions must finally ask 'was the product ever really the point?'

Her distinction between what 'can be generated' and what 'has to be formed', wisdom, judgment, character, the capacity to change one's mind, gives institutions a concrete filter for deciding which assignments AI has genuinely hollowed out versus which ones were never really testing a generatable product in the first place.

Shew explicitly refuses to export her own institution's playbook to a different context, naming the specific ways mission, student community, resources, language, and economic reality differ, a discipline against one-size-fits-all AI-strategy advice that many institutional leaders skip.

The host president's historical parallel, deliberately teaching computer skills before they were locally accessible, versus AI already being ubiquitous in students' pockets, reframes the institution's task from introducing a tool to teaching wise use of one students already have, which is a fundamentally different pedagogical problem.
quotes: This is forcing higher education to wrestle with a much deeper question, which isn't really about technology at all, but about formation: Was the product ever really the point?
Some things can be generated, while other things have to be formed. Wisdom, judgment, and character aren't acquired with a prompt, even a really good one.

But this particular place I'm working with isn't Lipscomb. Its mission is different and its students come from different communities. Its resources and residential culture are different. And its location in another country raises questions about access, language, culture, technology, and economic realities that we as a U.S. institution can't simply solve by exporting our own approach.

That means helping students question the output, recognize when it is wrong, notice whose knowledge and assumptions are represented, and discern when AI serves the work they are doing compared to when it allows them to bypass the very thinking and struggle the work was meant to cultivate.
The more I work on this presentation, the more I wonder whether one of the most important things an institution can do before developing an AI strategy is simply to know who it is.

They may be the ones that know most clearly what they are unwilling to outsource: the formation of wise people, rooted in a particular community, shaped by a particular mission, prepared to use powerful tools in service of something larger than themselves.
